subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: First Meeting with the Toy Shop

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites children to think about toys they love and briefly share one favourite toy aloud. This warms up listening and prediction before the story begins.

Teacher reads the story 'Talking Toys' aloud expressively from Textbook pp. 44–49, pausing at each new customer to let children absorb which toys are hoping to be chosen. Voices for the toy kitten, talking doll, and toy elephant may be used to bring the text alive.
Teacher continues reading pp. 50–55 aloud, covering the arrival of the final group of children and the cheerful ending. Children listen and track the sequence of buyers and toys.
A brief whole-class pause: teacher asks 'Which toy made you most curious and why?' — children respond with a word or short phrase, no full sentences needed yet.

periods.teacher_notes: The story gives voice to toys' emotions, so a lively read-aloud with varied tones for different toy characters draws children into the imaginative world quickly. Children unfamiliar with Chennapatna toys or Kondapalli dancing dolls may need a one-sentence naming note as those names come up in the text.

periods.activity_title: Reading Together: Shared Reading and Comprehension

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — A (p.49): name the toys and identify the little boy's chosen toy.

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads the opening paragraph of 'Talking Toys' (Textbook p. 44) together with the class, children joining in on any lines they remember from the earlier read-aloud.

Shared reading: teacher and children read pp. 44–49 together in segments — teacher reads a sentence, children echo or read along. Teacher pauses after each customer visit to check which toys were mentioned.

Let us think — A (p.49): teacher displays the two questions on the board. Children discuss question 1 (toys in the shop) in pairs for a brief moment, then the class compiles a collective list. Teacher then poses question 2 (the little boy's request) and children locate the answer in the text.
Children write their answers to both questions in their notebooks in one or two sentences each. Teacher circulates to confirm that answers are drawn directly from the story text.

periods.teacher_notes: The toy list is long — wooden toys, soft toys, board games, bats and balls, talking doll, toy elephant, Vande Bharat toy train, toy aeroplane, marbles, spinning top, dancing dolls — so prompting children to re-scan the text rather than recall from memory avoids incomplete lists. The Vande Bharat toy train is the specific answer to question 2 and can be confirmed by pointing children to the relevant passage.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — B (p.49): pair talk on feelings when given a toy and sharing about 'Jaadui Pitara'.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recalls the moment in the story when the toy elephant and talking doll each hoped to be chosen, asking children how they think those toys felt. This opens the door to talking about their own feelings around toys.

Let us think — B, question 1 (p.49): children sit in pairs and take turns describing how they feel when someone buys or gives them a toy. Teacher provides a sentence-starter on the board: 'When I get a toy, I feel…' and circulates to support quieter speakers.

Let us think — B, question 2 (p.49): teacher asks 'Have you seen the Jaadui Pitara?' — children share in pairs, then two or three pairs report to the whole class. Teacher adds a sentence about what the Jaadui Pitara is for those who have not encountered it.
Whole-class share: three or four children stand and share one feeling word and one memory about receiving a toy. Teacher echoes their ideas using full sentences to model oral expression.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have strong experiences with toys will speak readily; those who are quieter may benefit from the sentence-starter on the board as a scaffold. The Jaadui Pitara question is open-ended — accept any honest response and use it to briefly connect learning materials to the idea of playful discovery.

periods.activity_title: Listening to 'My Top' and Joining In

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen — A (p.51): listen to 'My Top' poem, then repeat along with teacher.

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks children to close their eyes and imagine a spinning top — what colours might it be, what sound does it make? Brief sharing of one or two responses, then teacher announces the poem 'My Top'.

Listening band: teacher reads 'My Top' aloud from Textbook p.51 at a measured pace — two clear repetitions, pointing to the text. Children listen only during the first reading; on the second they may hum along or tap the rhythm quietly.

Recitation: teacher reads one line, children repeat it as a class — choral echo for all six lines. The sequence is run through three times in full, building confidence and accuracy. Teacher watches for correct pronunciation of 'round and round' and 'jump around'.
Children recite the whole poem together without the teacher leading, using the text on p.51 as a prompt if needed. One volunteer may try a solo recitation, and the class echoes the last two lines.
Quick reflection: teacher asks what colours the poem mentions and children call them out. This bridges to the word-work activity on colour words.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem is short and rhythmic, so three full run-throughs of the echo pattern are usually enough for most children to feel secure reciting it. The colours red, green, yellow, and brown appear explicitly in the poem and will be revisited when children do the colour-word task in a later sitting.

periods.activity_title: Describing Words: Adjectives in the Story

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — A (p.50): add describing words from the help box to naming words.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn — A (p.50): write two more describing word + naming word pairs of your own.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'happy boy', 'pretty doll', 'blue frock', 'red cap' on the board — all drawn from the story's language — and asks: which word tells us more about the toy or person? Children identify the describing word in each pair.

Teacher introduces the concept: words like happy, red, blue, talking tell us more about naming words and are called describing words. Children find two more describing-word examples from Textbook pp. 44–49 and share with a partner.

Let us learn — A (p.50): teacher displays the Help Box words (brown, clean, cold, white, cotton, large) on the board. Children work individually to add a suitable describing word to each naming word — food, kurta, water, paper, tree. Teacher circulates and prompts children to read each pair aloud to check that it sounds right.
Pairs compare answers and discuss any where they chose different words. Teacher confirms that more than one describing word may fit a naming word and that this is acceptable.

periods.teacher_notes: The story is rich with describing words — 'talking doll', 'toy elephant', 'spinning top', 'dancing dolls' — so returning children to the text to find their own examples before the task helps them see the concept in context rather than in isolation. The Help Box task has multiple acceptable answers for some blanks; accept any that make sense and have children read the pair aloud as a self-check.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn — B (p.50): write plurals by adding 's' to cat, cup, doll, shop, train.
Let us learn — C (p.51): write plurals by adding 'es' to class, bus, pouch, brush, mango.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'toy → toys' and 'boy → boys' on the board, drawing attention to these pairs from the story. Children read them aloud and identify what changed — the addition of 's' to make more than one.

Let us learn — B (p.50): children write the plural of cat, cup, doll, shop, train in their notebooks. Teacher calls on five different children to write one answer each on the board. The class reads the plural words aloud together, saying both the singular and the plural.

Teacher introduces the -es rule using 'box → boxes' from Textbook p.51, asking children to listen to the sound at the end of 'class', 'bus', 'pouch', 'brush', 'mango'. They clap once on the last sound to feel whether a new syllable is added when -s alone would be said.

Let us learn — C (p.51): children write the -es plurals for class, bus, pouch, brush, mango in their notebooks. Teacher writes the answers on the board and children self-check, reading each pair (singular → plural) aloud.
Quick oral consolidation: teacher says a word and children call out the plural — three -s words, then three -es words — as a fast whole-class chant.

periods.teacher_notes: The -es rule can feel arbitrary to children, so connecting it to the sound test — does adding only 's' create an awkward ending? — helps them generalise rather than memorise. 'Mango → mangoes' follows the same rule and also appears in the story context of the market, giving a natural anchor.

periods.activity_title: Colour Words in the Poem 'My Top'

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen — B (p.52): circle colour words from the list that appear in 'My Top'.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recites 'My Top' from Textbook p.51 once, then asks children to close their eyes and picture the top spinning. Teacher asks: what colours did you see in your mind? Children share freely — answers need not match the poem yet.

Teacher writes all eight colour words on the board: red, pink, green, blue, yellow, white, brown, purple. Children read them aloud together. Teacher asks children to look at Textbook p.51 and scan the poem to find which of these colours are actually named there.

Let us listen — B (p.52): teacher directs children to the task. Children circle the colour words from the given list that appear in 'My Top'. Teacher reads the poem aloud once more as children check their circled words against each line.

Whole-class check: teacher asks 'Which colours did you circle?' — children call out: red, green, yellow, brown. Teacher confirms these four are in the poem. Brief discussion: why are pink, blue, white, purple not circled? Children explain in their own words.
Children write a sentence in their notebooks using one of the four poem-colour words and a naming word of their choice — e.g. 'a red top' or 'a yellow mango'. One or two read aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: Having chanted the poem together in an earlier sitting, most children will recognise the colour words from memory; this task asks them to verify through the text, practising careful reading rather than relying solely on recall. Pink, blue, white, and purple are deliberate distractors in the list and help children distinguish what is in the text from what they might imagine.

periods.activity_title: Sequencing Sentences: How the Mother Bird Made a Kite

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — A (pp. 52–53): complete sentence frames about the mother bird making a kite.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the six picture clues from Textbook p.52 one at a time, asking children to describe aloud what they see in each illustration — the baby bird, the mother collecting spider-web thread, gum from a tree, and the palm leaf blade. This builds the vocabulary children will need before writing.

Teacher reads the incomplete 'Making a Kite' sentence frames from Textbook p.53 aloud and writes the clue words on the board: onion peel, thread from spider web, gum from a tree, leaf blade from the palm tree. Class discusses together which clue fits the first blank — 'The mother bird brought ___ from onions' — and teacher writes the agreed answer.

Children complete the remaining three sentence frames independently in their notebooks, using the pictures on p.52 and the clue words on the board to sequence the steps correctly. Teacher circulates and supports children who are unsure of the order by asking them to point to the matching picture for each sentence.

Three children read their completed sentences aloud in order. Class checks whether the four sentences together tell the kite-making story from beginning to end. Any differences are discussed briefly and corrected.

periods.teacher_notes: The sequencing depends on reading the pictures carefully — children who rush past the illustrations may muddle the middle two steps (spider-web thread and gum from a tree), so pointing to the matching picture for each sentence before writing is a useful prompt. The final sentence 'Finally, ___' should describe the baby bird flying the kite, which is clearly shown in the last illustration.

periods.activity_title: Letter Art: Drawing a Bird from the Letter B

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — B (p.54): follow seven steps to draw and colour a bird from the letter 'B'.
Let us write — C (p.54): draw a picture using any other letter of the alphabet.

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes a large capital 'B' on the board and asks children what they notice about its shape — two bumps, a straight back. Teacher previews the activity: they will turn this letter into a bird, step by step, using the guide on Textbook p.54.

Let us write — B (p.54): teacher demonstrates each of the seven steps slowly on the board while children follow along in their notebooks — writing B, adding the beak (sleeping v), drawing the eye with a dot, adding the wing (w shape), drawing the tail, adding feet and a small branch. Children colour their bird at step 7.

Let us write — C (p.54): children choose any other letter of the alphabet and try to draw a picture from it, following the same creative process they just practised. Teacher moves around the room encouraging imaginative choices and helping children who are uncertain which letter to pick.
Quick gallery: children hold up their letter-picture creations. Teacher acknowledges two or three interesting choices and asks those children to name the letter they used and what they made from it.

periods.teacher_notes: The letter-art task develops fine-motor control and creative thinking together; children who finish the 'B' bird quickly should move straight to the free letter choice. Encourage children to try letters with curves (C, D, G, O, S) as well as straight-line letters, since the variety makes the gallery share richer.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do (p.55): make a jute or cardboard face puppet following the eight-step guide.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the story: the toys in the market each had a face and a personality — now children will make their own toy character. Teacher briefly shows the eight-step guide on Textbook p.55 and names the materials on the table.

Teacher walks through all eight steps once without children drawing, pointing to each illustration on p.55 — tracing the face outline, cutting, drawing features, colouring, adding woollen hair, and attaching the handle. Children ask any clarifying questions before beginning.

Children follow the eight steps to make their puppets — tracing and cutting the face shape, drawing eyes, nose, and mouth, colouring the face, gluing woollen thread for hair, and attaching a handle. Teacher circulates, steadying cardboard for cutting if needed and encouraging individual choices in colour and expression.

Children hold up their finished puppets. Teacher invites two or three children to give their puppet a name and say one thing about its personality in a sentence — linking back to the talking toys in the story.

periods.teacher_notes: Pre-cutting the cardboard or jute into face-sized pieces before the sitting saves time and ensures every child can complete all eight steps within the available minutes. Children who finish early can decorate the back of the handle with their name or a small pattern.
materials: Jute sheets or cardboard pieces (pre-cut to face size)

periods.activity_title: Bringing the Toy Shop to Life: A Chapter Celebration

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a brisk whole-class quiz on the story: name a toy that hoped to be chosen, name the Indian toy traditions mentioned, say what -es plurals three shop items might have. Children respond chorally or with hands raised, drawing on the story and the language work they know.

Retelling circle: children sit in a circle and retell the story of the toy shop together — one child begins with the opening of the market, and each child around the circle adds the next customer group or toy event, using describing words and plural forms naturally in their telling.

Independent writing: each child writes two or three sentences imagining they are a new toy arriving in the market — what they look like (using a describing word), what they hope a child will do, and how they feel. Children use their notebooks and write without a scaffold, drawing on the story's language.

Children recite 'My Top' together in two groups — one group says the first three lines, the other responds with the last three — then swap. This revisits the poem's colour words and rhythm as a joyful close to the chapter's oracy work.

Gallery and share: children who made puppets (or drew letter-art birds) hold them up while two or three volunteers read their toy-voice sentences aloud. Teacher names the Indian toy traditions — Chennapatna toys, Kondapalli dancing dolls, Vande Bharat Train — once more as a closing salute to the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: The retelling circle works best when the teacher gently redirects children who skip a customer group back to the story sequence — wooden toys, soft toys, board games, bats and balls are all in the opening inventory, and the customer visits follow a clear order. The independent writing task is intentionally open; accept any toy voice, real or invented, as long as it carries a describing word and a feeling.

items.source_context: Toy shop story: toys' names, customers, and the little boy's Vande Bharat train request.
items.item_stem:
Read the sentences below. Write True or False for each one.
1. The toy shop in the story sells only soft toys and board games.
2. A little boy asked his mother to buy him a Vande Bharat toy train.
3. The toy kitten was the first to be bought by a customer.
4. At the end of the story, all the toys in the shop were sold.

options.text: A little boy asked his mother to buy him a Vande Bharat toy train.
At the end of the story, all the toys in the shop were sold.
The toy kitten was the first to be bought by a customer.
The toy shop in the story sells only soft toys and board games.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. False — the shop stocks wooden toys, soft toys, board games, bats and balls, and more. 2. True — the little boy asked his mother for a Vande Bharat toy train and she bought it. 3. False — the toy kitten was not bought; the first toy mentioned as being purchased is the Vande Bharat toy train. 4. False — the story does not say every toy was sold; only selected toys were chosen by customers.

Matches each toy to the correct buyer or group.
Uses the story's language naturally in the response.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will read the poem 'My Top' aloud from Textbook page 51 twice. Listen carefully. Then answer: How many colours are named in the poem, and which colour is mentioned first?

options.label: A
options.text: Four colours; brown is mentioned first.

options.label: B
options.text: Four colours; red is mentioned first.

options.label: C
options.text: Three colours; yellow is mentioned first.

options.label: D
options.text: Two colours; green is mentioned first.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have counted only the colours in one line and missed the next line's pair.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student likely recalled only the first two colour words and did not listen through the whole poem.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student correctly recalled the number of colours but confused the order in which they appear in the poem.

items.item_stem: The sentences below describe how the mother bird made a kite, but they are in the wrong order. Write the numbers 1 to 4 to show the correct order.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Sentence | Correct order |
|---|---|
| Finally, the baby bird flew the kite. | |
| The mother bird brought peel from onions. | |
| Next, the mother bird got a leaf blade from the palm tree. | |
| Then, she found thread from a spider web. | |

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1-b, 2-c, 3-d, 4-a (using row order: Finally = 4, Onion peel = 1, Palm leaf = 3, Spider web = 2).

answer_key.left: Finally, the baby bird flew the kite.
The mother bird brought peel from onions.
Next, the mother bird got a leaf blade from the palm tree.
Then, she found thread from a spider web.
